Read as Markdown · For people and coding agents

Building WebAssembly (WASM) providers

Build a small Rust component that publishes JSON to Moonframe, then read it from a Luau view and send it messages. This guide is for people writing a provider by hand and coding agents building one for an app.

A provider supplies data; a mod draws it. A provider in providers/counter/ publishes as app.counter, and mods address it as provider:counter. Moonframe runs each WASM provider in its own sandbox with Wasmtime. You do not rebuild or restart the Moonframe executable to add one.

Choose a provider kind

Need Kind
Transform data, keep an in-memory model, or use a host capability wasm
Publish a sample JSON file without running code static
Run a CLI, read files, make HTTP requests, or reuse a Python/Node program process
Use the host app's Rust libraries or asynchronous services directly native

WASM providers cannot read your files, use the network, inherit your environment, or spawn processes. The built-in machine-data capability is system (CPU, memory and network counters); moonframe.page renders a public web page for it (below), and moonframe.view reads a mod's view and acts on it (below). Embedding apps can register namespaced capabilities such as mshub.entities. There are no built-in http, fs or exec capabilities. Process and native providers run with the user's access instead. See the library guide for native providers.

Rust is the path Moonframe builds automatically. Other languages work if they produce a WebAssembly Component Model component implementing the same WIT interface; a plain core WASM module is not enough.

Set up the folder

You need Moonframe with its default wasm feature enabled, Rust/Cargo, and the WASI Preview 2 target:

rustup target add wasm32-wasip2

Use a current stable Rust toolchain (the example uses edition 2024). In the Moonframe repository, use its pinned rust-toolchain.toml.

Choose the folder that already holds your app's main.luau:

Working on App folder
The cloned starter or an app on the Rust library app/ in that project
A profile made with moonframe app new The profile project root
Your installed Moonframe ~/.config/moonframe (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/moonframe)

For an installed app, write to the user's folder, not inside the signed application bundle. In the commands below, run from this app folder. Pick an unused provider name: a user provider replaces a built-in provider with the same folder name. Names use lowercase a-z, digits, - and _.

Create this layout:

providers/counter/
  provider.toml
  Cargo.toml
  src/lib.rs
  wit/provider.wit
mods/wasm-counter/
  main.luau

mkdir -p providers/counter/src providers/counter/wit mods/wasm-counter

Copy wit/provider.wit from the Moonframe version you are using into providers/counter/wit/provider.wit. In a cloned starter, from app/:

cp ../wit/provider.wit providers/counter/wit/provider.wit

For a separate project, obtain that file from the matching Moonframe release tag or commit. Keep a local copy in the provider so it builds wherever its folder is copied. WIT is the interface definition shared by the component and the host; do not invent or change its exports.

Declare the provider

Write providers/counter/provider.toml:

kind = "wasm"
interval = 1.0
capabilities = []

[settings]
initial = 0

The folder name determines app.counter, not the Cargo package name. Manifest fields for a WASM provider are:

Field Meaning
kind Must be "wasm"; no command or file field.
interval Seconds to wait for a message before calling tick; defaults to 1.0, allowed range 0.1–3600.0.
start "on-demand" (default), or "always" to start with the app.
capabilities An empty list by default; "system", Moonframe's own ("moonframe.page", "moonframe.view"), and names registered by the embedding host. Unknown names are manifest errors.
[settings] Your configuration, converted to JSON and passed to start.

Unknown manifest fields are errors. Keep provider-specific configuration under [settings].

Write providers/counter/Cargo.toml:

[package]
name = "counter"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
publish = false

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
serde_json = "1"
wit-bindgen = "0.63"

[profile.release]
lto = true
opt-level = "s"
strip = true

[workspace]

The empty [workspace] makes this an independent crate, even inside the host's Rust workspace. Keep the generated Cargo.lock in source control. Leave the library filename at its default: Moonframe locates the output using the package name, replacing hyphens with underscores.

Implement the component

Write providers/counter/src/lib.rs:

use std::cell::RefCell;
use serde_json::{Value, json};

wit_bindgen::generate!({ path: "wit/provider.wit", world: "provider" });

struct Counter;

#[derive(Default)]
struct State {
    initial: u32,
    count: u32,
}

thread_local! {
    static STATE: RefCell<State> = RefCell::new(State::default());
}

fn snapshot(state: &State) -> String {
    json!({ "count": state.count }).to_string()
}

impl Guest for Counter {
    fn start(settings: String) -> Result<(), String> {
        let settings: Value = serde_json::from_str(&settings)
            .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?;
        let initial = match settings.get("initial") {
            None => 0,
            Some(value) => value.as_u64()
                .and_then(|value| u32::try_from(value).ok())
                .ok_or("initial must be an integer from 0 to 4294967295")?,
        };
        STATE.with_borrow_mut(|state| *state = State { initial, count: initial });
        Ok(())
    }

    fn tick() -> Option<String> {
        Some(STATE.with_borrow(snapshot))
    }

    fn receive(message: String) -> Option<String> {
        let message: Value = serde_json::from_str(&message).ok()?;
        STATE.with_borrow_mut(|state| {
            if message.get("add").and_then(Value::as_bool) == Some(true) {
                state.count = state.count.saturating_add(1);
            } else if message.get("reset").and_then(Value::as_bool) == Some(true) {
                state.count = state.initial;
            } else {
                return None;
            }
            Some(snapshot(state))
        })
    }
}

export!(Counter);

wit-bindgen generates the Guest trait and export! macro from the WIT file. Implement all three exports:

Export Called when Result
start(settings) Once per component instance, before the first tick Ok(()), or Err(message) to fail startup.
tick() Immediately after startup, then after each interval without a message Some(json) publishes a snapshot; None keeps the previous value.
receive(message) A mod sends a message to the provider Some(json) publishes immediately; None keeps the previous value.

Frequent messages can postpone periodic ticks: interval is an idle timeout, not a fixed-rate timer. Keep work bounded and return promptly.

Each publication replaces app.counter; it is not a partial merge. Return the whole object the views need. JSON objects become Luau tables, arrays become lists, and null becomes nil. Publications are limited to 1 MiB of JSON, 10,000 values and nesting depth 16 (the root is depth 0). Invalid JSON or a component trap stops the provider and reports a problem.

Messages contain the payload alone. The button below sends {"add":true} to receive, not a {"from":...,"message":...} envelope. That envelope belongs to process providers. WASM's current interface does not expose the sender or provide native-provider reply routing; publish results for views or provider/counter subscribers to consume.

The STATE value survives calls, but resets when a new build replaces the provider, unless it keeps its state. It is saved across launches for namespaced entries using stateful-provider (below). Ordinary app-folder providers keep their existing reload-only behavior. Use a mod's persisted state for UI choices that should survive quitting.

Keep state across a new build

Editing a provider rebuilds and restarts it. To carry its state over, as a mod's state is across a reload, generate the bindings from the stateful-provider world and add two exports:

wit_bindgen::generate!({ path: "wit/provider.wit", world: "stateful-provider" });

// In `impl Guest for Counter`:
fn save() -> Option<String> {
    Some(STATE.with_borrow(snapshot))
}

fn restore(state: String) -> Result<(), String> {
    let saved: Value = serde_json::from_str(&state)
        .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?;
    let count = saved.get("count")
        .and_then(Value::as_u64)
        .and_then(|count| u32::try_from(count).ok())
        .ok_or("no count in the saved state")?;
    STATE.with_borrow_mut(|state| state.count = count);
    Ok(())
}
Export Called when Result
save() This build stops, because a new one replaces it Some(text) hands it to the next build; None keeps nothing.
restore(state) On a new build, after start and before the first tick Ok(()), or Err(message) to start fresh.

The state is any text, usually JSON, up to 1 MiB. Ordinary app-folder providers keep it in memory for this launch. External entries also save it atomically on clean shutdown under the app's state directory, keyed by namespace and id; moving the entry's folder does not change its identity. --no-user keeps no durable state. Headless hosts set ProviderOptions::state_dir explicitly. start still runs first, so settings stay current: restore only what the user built up. Plain provider components keep working and start over. examples/research/providers/research is a working example, including how to let a changed setting win over the saved state.

  • Your state changed shape. Read what you can in restore, with defaults for what is new. Return Err if nothing fits: the provider starts fresh and the reason goes to the terminal log. The saved state is then gone.
  • A build fails. A build or instantiation error leaves the previous worker answering messages and publishing data, with stale status. Once the new component instantiates, the old one saves and stops. A panic in restore or the first tick retains the saved state for the next attempt.
  • A running provider panics. It has nothing left to save, so the next build starts fresh. Only state from a clean stop is handed on.

Compile it into the app

A provider written against the guest SDK builds either way from the same source: as a component, sandboxed and rebuilt as you edit, or linked into the app as an ordinary crate, with no wasmtime, Cargo or sandbox at run time.

// providers/counter/src/lib.rs
use {moonframe_provider::Provider, serde_json::Value};

pub struct Counter(u64);

impl Provider for Counter {
    fn start(_settings: Value) -> Result<Self, String> {
        Ok(Self(0))
    }

    fn tick(&mut self) -> Option<Value> {
        self.0 += 1;
        Some(self.0.into())
    }

    fn receive(&mut self, message: Value) -> Option<Value> {
        (message == "reset").then(|| { self.0 = 0; self.0.into() })
    }
}

moonframe_provider::export!(Counter); // the component's exports; nothing natively

Give the crate crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"] so the app can depend on it, then register it under the folder's name and switch the folder's kind:

Moonframe::new(...).native("counter", moonframe::Portable::<counter::Counter>::new)

# providers/counter/provider.toml
kind = "native"     # was "wasm"; the rest stays as it was

Compiled in, it is called in the same order (start, restore, a first tick published at once, then ticks and messages) and log, system_load and host_call reach the app with the same capabilities from provider.toml (system needs the app's system or wasm feature). What differs: it has the user's access and no fuel or memory limits, so link only code you would run yourself; save hands state to the next start only within one launch; and a change needs the app rebuilt.

examples/portable is a complete example to copy: a focus timer crate in app/providers/focus (settings, ticks, messages, save/restore, and unit tests that run natively), run as a component from that folder and compiled in for app/providers/focus-native, side by side in one window. Its host/ binary sits beside the app folder, not around it: Cargo counts any crate inside a workspace member's folder as a member, so a provider crate there could not keep its own [workspace]. examples/capability-provider builds both ways too.

How the two builds compare

examples/portable/host/examples/bench runs providers both ways through the provider runtime the app uses, so the numbers are what a view waits for. All figures are medians, from three runs on an Apple M4 Max (macOS, release build).

Calls and startup. The example's focus timer does almost no work per call, so this is the runtime's own cost:

Wasm Native
Start, to the first data 15.6 ms prebuilt (provider.wasm); 236 ms from source, Cargo finding nothing to build; 7.2 s for the first build 0.2 ms
Message to published answer, median 8.6 µs 7.0 µs
Same, p99 17.4 µs 13.5 µs
Messages per second, one at a time about 109,000 about 145,000

Most of a round trip is the hop to the provider's thread and back, which both builds share; Wasm adds about 1.5 µs a call. Startup differs more: wasmtime compiles the component each time it starts (160 KiB here), and a provider built from source asks Cargo first.

A real workload. examples/portable/bench/providers/digest does what Wasm providers are for, shaping data: each cycle it fetches a batch of request-log lines through a host capability, parses every line, folds numeric path segments into :id, works out per-route counts, error rates and p50/p95/p99 latencies, and publishes the 50 busiest routes. One cycle, message to published summary (the opt-level = 3 column, in brackets in the last, is from one run):

Lines Batch Wasm, opt-level = "s" Wasm, opt-level = 3 Native Wasm ÷ native
1,000 59 KiB 0.7 ms 0.5 ms 0.3 ms 2.4× (1.7×)
10,000 596 KiB 4.5 ms 3.3 ms 1.8 ms 2.5× (1.8×)
50,000 2.9 MiB 21.6 ms 15.2 ms 8.9 ms 2.4× (1.7×)

Moving the lines alone (fetching without digesting, measured in one run each) is 1.5× slower in Wasm (1.3× at opt-level = 3), so the parsing and sorting itself runs about 3× slower, or 2× when optimised for speed. The repository's providers build with opt-level = "s" for small components; for one that computes much, use opt-level = 3 in its [profile.release].

What this means:

  • At an interval of seconds, either build is fast enough: even 50,000 lines a cycle is 22 ms of work as a component.
  • Compiling in pays off for an app that starts often or runs many providers, and for a provider that digests large batches often: 50,000 lines every half second is about 4% of a core as a component, 2% compiled in.
  • A Wasm provider's results cross as JSON text, so a float can come back one bit away from the native build's: the host parses JSON with serde_json's fast float parser.
  • A host call carries at most 1 MiB by default; the 50,000-line batch is 2.9 MiB, so the bench raises HostCallLimits::max_bytes (for both builds).

Run it yourself (it needs rustup target add wasm32-wasip2):

cargo run --release -p moonframe-portable-example --example bench

Host-defined capabilities and external miniapps

An embedding app can expose a narrow JSON API to Wasm:

use moonframe::{Caller, HostCapability, Moonframe, RootPolicy};

struct Entities;
impl HostCapability for Entities {
    fn call(&self, caller: &Caller, method: &str, args: &str) -> Result<String, String> {
        // Authorize using this loader-supplied identity, never an id in args.
        if caller.provider != "mshub:notes" || method != "echo" {
            return Err("not allowed".into());
        }
        Ok(args.to_owned())
    }
}

let app = Moonframe::new("mshub")
    .app_dir("app")
    .capability("mshub.entities", Entities)
    .root("mshub", "/path/to/miniapps", RootPolicy::default())
    .entry("mshub", "notes", "/path/to/miniapps/notes")
    .on_entry_status(|status| eprintln!("{}: {:?}", status.name, status.state));
let entries = app.entry_handle(); // Clone into host threads before app.run().
// After the host's own platform/enabled filtering:
entries.add_entry("mshub", "tasks", "/path/to/tasks")?;
entries.remove_entry("mshub", "tasks");

Roots register a namespace, path and policy; they do not scan. Use the Entries handle's add_root / remove_root and add_entry / remove_entry to control exactly what loads at runtime. Each entry may have main.luau, provider/provider.toml, or both. Entry paths are chosen by the trusted host and may lie outside the root directory. Guests cannot change this registry.

The name is exactly <namespace>:<id>:

  • ui.mount "mshub:notes", or ui.mount { "mshub:notes", id = "second" };
  • app["mshub:notes"], to = "provider:mshub:notes";
  • subscribe = { "provider/mshub:notes" };
  • persisted mod/instance keys include mshub:notes (for example mod:mshub:notes#second). Removing an entry does not erase its saved state.

Namespace and id each use 1–48 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, -, _. Namespaces app, provider, topic, demo, component, shell and parent are reserved because those prefixes route messages elsewhere. : is supported in topics and persistence keys. Entry edits are watched like app-folder edits, including in release bundles; invalid mod parse/init/first-view edits keep the previous working code. Native code is compiled into the host: register .native("mshub:notes", factory) and put kind = "native" in that entry's provider manifest. There is no runtime native-library loading.

RootPolicy::default() uses BuildPolicy::PrebuiltOnly and disables process and socket providers. Prebuilt-only entries require provider.wasm and reject Cargo.toml, even when both are present. For reviewed development sources use RootPolicy { build: BuildPolicy::Cargo, ..Default::default() }; Cargo still refuses local build.rs and .cargo/ hooks. allow_process and allow_socket are explicit opt-ins. Ordinary app layers retain their existing behavior.

An entry may also bring components/<name>.luau and style.luau:

notes/
  main.luau            the mod, mounted as ui.mount "mshub:notes"
  style.luau           optional: return style { rules = { ... } }
  components/
    card.luau          use "card" finds this before the app's `card`
  provider/
    provider.toml

The entry's use looks in its own components/ first, then in the app's; other mods never see an entry's components, and they stay out of the Components window. Its style.luau takes only rules, which apply to what the entry draws (under its mod's own styles, over the app's stylesheet) and may name the app's colors; colors, fonts and the other stylesheet keys belong to the app and are refused. Both reload live with the entry; a broken style.luau keeps its last good rules and reports through on_entry_status.

Built-in miniapps. A miniapp shipped inside the host binary needs no files on disk: embed its folder with rust-embed and select it with entry_embedded. It is written to ~/.cache/<app>/entries/<namespace>/<id>/<hash> as the app starts (once per content), so main.luau, components/ and a kind = "native" provider work in a release bundle. In debug, point entry at the source folder instead, for live reload, as with embedded_app and app_dir:

#[derive(moonframe::rust_embed::RustEmbed)]
#[crate_path = "moonframe::rust_embed"]
#[folder = "miniapps/notes"]
struct Notes;

let app = Moonframe::new("mshub").root("builtin", "miniapps", RootPolicy::default());
let app = if cfg!(debug_assertions) {
    app.entry("builtin", "notes", concat!(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"), "/miniapps/notes"))
} else {
    app.entry_embedded::<Notes>("builtin", "notes")
};

On the runtime handle, use moonframe::EmbeddedEntries and call entries.add_entry_embedded::<Notes>("builtin", "notes"); one added before run waits until the app knows its cache folder.

Checking an entry. moonframe::check_entry(path, &policy, &options) returns a Vec<Diagnostic> (severity, file, line, message) for a host CLI's <app> miniapp check. It loads main.luau, components and style.luau, draws the view with no data and then with each case CheckOptions gives (fake app tables, starting states, messages), reads provider/provider.toml with its capabilities checked against options.capabilities, and applies policy. An entry that ships a sample.json (beside main.luau or in provider/) is drawn with it as its provider's data, so a branch that only draws once data arrives is checked: ship one. See checking what miniapps draw for every option, live diagnostics, snapshots and headless renders.

EntryStatus contains name, kind (Mod/Provider), state (Ok/Building/Stale/Failed), optional error, revision (an opaque fingerprint of the attempted revision, not a monotonic counter), and view_errors: what the entry's views drew wrong, as ViewDiagnostics, sent when they change and empty once the view draws cleanly. The callback runs on the loading thread; keep it short. Wasm build/instantiate progress and errors use this callback. It does not publish a topic. On-demand providers report once wanted. Headless integrations use Capabilities::capability, Manifest::load_with / check_with, and Providers::start_configured with ProviderOptions for capabilities, status and durable state.

In the guest's provider.toml:

kind = "wasm"
capabilities = ["mshub.entities"]

Both WIT worlds import host-call(capability, method, args) -> result<string, string>. system-load is unchanged, including for old prebuilt components. Undeclared calls return Err without invoking the host. Capability names must be namespaced with dots; unprefixed names and moonframe.* are reserved. Caller includes the registered provider name, provider folder, root path, optional namespace, and all declared capability names.

The standalone Rust guest SDK is crates/moonframe-provider (add it as a path or git dependency). Implement moonframe_provider::Provider and export it with moonframe_provider::export!(MyProvider); the same crate can then be compiled into the app too (see Compile it into the app). Enable its stateful feature for save/restore. The raw WIT bindings stay available on wasm32 as moonframe_provider::bindings. Its typed helper serializes arguments and deserializes the JSON answer:

let answer: serde_json::Value = moonframe_provider::host_call(
    "mshub.entities", "echo", &serde_json::json!({ "id": 42 }),
)?;

examples/capability-provider is a complete guest using example.echo; register that name in its host. For asynchronous services implement AsyncHostCapability and use .capability_async(...); it uses the existing .tokio(handle) runtime. Configure .host_call_limits(HostCallLimits { ... }) as needed: defaults are 1 MiB each for arguments/results, 5 seconds per call, and 32 outstanding host calls. Host work consumes no Wasm fuel. Timeout, panic, invalid JSON and size errors return strings to the guest. Async timeouts drop the future; synchronous Rust cannot be forcibly cancelled, so a timed-out call may finish later. Until it finishes that instance cannot start another host call, and it still counts toward the outstanding-call limit. Host APIs should account for this when implementing writes.

Draw it and send messages

Write mods/wasm-counter/main.luau:

return mod {
    region = "right",
    view = function(state, app)
        local counter = app.counter
        if not counter then
            return ui.text "Waiting for the WASM counter…"
        end
        return ui.panel {
            title = "WASM counter",
            ui.column {
                ui.text(`Count: {counter.count}`),
                ui.button { "Add one", to = "provider:counter", msg = { add = true } },
                ui.button { "Reset", to = "provider:counter", msg = { reset = true } },
            },
        }
    end,
}

The starter shell places mods from the right region automatically. A custom shell must include that region or mount wasm-counter explicitly. Handle app.counter == nil while the component builds or before it publishes its first value.

Reading app.counter from a drawn view starts the provider on demand. Subscribing to provider/counter or sending a message also starts it. Once started, it keeps running even if the view is hidden. Use start = "always" only when it should work before any mod needs it.

Declare its types

Without types, app.counter is any to the Luau checker: a view that reads a field the provider never publishes, or sends it a message it ignores, passes just types and fails quietly at runtime. Declare both in providers/counter/types.luau:

-- What app.counter holds.
export type Published = {
    count: number,
}

-- What send "provider:counter" takes.
export type Message = { add: boolean } | { reset: boolean }

Then send with send, which builds the same { to = ..., msg = ... } a literal would, so its message is checked:

update = function(state, msg)
    return state, { send "provider:counter" { add = true } }
end,

just types DIR checks the app's mods against them: reading counter.total, or sending { ad = true }, is a type error with its line. For a provider in the starter's app/providers/, just provider-types also copies them into types/moonframe.d.luau, so every app sees them; just provider-types-check (in just ci) fails when that copy is stale.

Keep an example of what it publishes beside them as published.json, and hold both sides to it: just provider-types-check fails when the file's keys or kinds differ from Published, and a test in the crate compares a real tick against it (see examples/portable/app/providers/focus). Then neither the Rust nor the Luau side can change without the other.

Limits: only Published's own fields are held to the example, a level deep; button msg = ..., to = ... and plain { to = ..., msg = ... } tables are not checked, only send; and the type names (Published) are not visible in mods, whose own annotations are checked against them by shape. Nothing checks the published JSON at runtime.

Build, run and check

From the app folder, compile the exact component:

cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip2 \
  --manifest-path providers/counter/Cargo.toml \
  --target-dir target/providers

The output is target/providers/wasm32-wasip2/release/counter.wasm. This target produces a component; wasm32-unknown-unknown does not produce the required artifact. You do not need cargo component for this example.

Check and run using the command for your app:

App Validate UI and manifests Open the app
Cloned starter (from repository root) just check and just types just run
Linked profile moonframe --profile NAME --check moonframe --profile NAME
App on the library (from Rust project root) cargo run -- --check cargo run
Installed starter with user mods moonframe --check moonframe

--check does not compile or execute WASM providers. A passing check validates the manifest and Luau but is not a runtime test. Build the component too, then verify in the running app:

  1. The panel shows Count: 0 (or your configured initial).
  2. Add one updates the count immediately; Reset restores initial.
  3. Changing initial in provider.toml restarts this provider with the new value.
  4. Editing src/lib.rs rebuilds it; a compile error shows as a provider problem.
  5. With save and restore, the count survives that edit.

Agents should report which checks they ran and which runtime interactions still need the user's verification.

When Cargo.toml and Cargo are available, Moonframe builds the source automatically on startup and when the provider's folder changes. Builds go to the app's cache (the starter uses ~/.cache/moonframe/providers, or its $XDG_CACHE_HOME equivalent). Only the changed provider restarts; the window and other providers keep running. Changes to dependencies outside the provider folder may require a manual reload.

A failed source build is an error, even if an older provider.wasm exists. Without source or without Cargo, Moonframe loads provider.wasm from the provider folder instead. If neither path is available, startup fails.

Host calls and limits

To log a diagnostic, use the generated host interface:

moonframe::provider::host::log("counter started");

This moonframe module comes from wit-bindgen, not a dependency on the Moonframe Rust library. Logs go through the host's logging system; run the app from a terminal to inspect them. Publishing happens through the return value of tick or receive, not println!.

For machine load, put capabilities = ["system"] at the top level of provider.toml, before [settings], then call:

let sample = moonframe::provider::host::system_load()?;
let load: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_str(&sample)
    .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?;

This fragment belongs in a function returning Result<_, String>. Without the capability the call returns an error. cpu and memory are fractions from 0 to 1; memory_used and memory_total are bytes, and received and transmitted are bytes per second. See the complete system provider for collecting a bounded history and handling a failed host call.

Rendering a web page

moonframe.page loads a web page the way a reader sees it, with its scripts, in a hidden web view, and answers with its text and, when asked, a picture. List it, capabilities = ["moonframe.page"], then:

let page: serde_json::Value = moonframe_provider::host_call(
    "moonframe.page",
    "render",
    &serde_json::json!({ "url": "https://example.com", "screenshot": true }),
)?;

render takes url (http or https, no user name or password), screenshot (default false), width and height (the window it lays out in, 1280 by 900 points by default), timeout (seconds to load, 20 by default, at most 60) and drop (up to 64 CSS selectors left out of the text, such as ["nav", "footer"]). It answers url (where it ended up, after redirects), title, text (the rendered text, innerText, up to 2 MiB), truncated, timed_out (it had not finished loading in its time and was read as it showed), and with screenshot, screenshot (mime image/png, base64, width, height: what showed, width pixels wide whatever the screen's scale, up to 4 MiB) or screenshot_error. A page that does not load is an error.

The page gets a session of its own, kept nowhere, that reaches the public internet alone: every connection goes through the proxy a PDF of a web page uses, which refuses this machine and its network after each redirect and lookup, and WebRTC is off. Its calls have their own bounds (a minute and a quarter, about 8 MiB), not host_call_limits. Four render at once. It needs the browser feature and, so far, macOS; elsewhere the call answers why not.

Reading and driving a view

moonframe.view lets a provider look at a mod's view in the front main window as a person would describe it, and do one thing a person could do to it: test a page it wrote, or drive one for its user. List it, capabilities = ["moonframe.view"], then:

let page: serde_json::Value =
    moonframe_provider::host_call("moonframe.view", "tree", &serde_json::json!({ "mod": "notes" }))?;
let after: serde_json::Value = moonframe_provider::host_call(
    "moonframe.view",
    "act",
    &serde_json::json!({ "mod": "notes", "ref": "e0.3", "action": "fill", "value": "Groceries" }),
)?;

tree takes mod and answers tree, one line per element indented by depth (button "Save" [e0.3]), the same as nodes (ref, role, name, value, selected, disabled, depth), truncated past 2,000 elements or 128 KiB of names and values (each cut at 4,000 characters), and problems, what the mods it read report wrong. Components and mounted mods are read through, a mod that mounts itself once; text inside a clickable row names the row, and a field's value is the text it holds. Roles are button (a button or a clickable row), item, textbox, text, badge, panel, document (markdown), image, list, popover, dialog, terminal, browser, map, video, view and problem.

act takes mod, ref (from the last tree), action and its value, and answers the tree again, from the window it acted in. It sends what the element itself sends, as a person's act would: click (the element, or the nearest one around it that takes a click), fill (a field's text, in place of what it holds, typed into the field while it is drawn, which sends its change; a field with no id hears its change with the text, so give one an id to fill it as typing would), press (a key such as enter, escape or cmd-k: the field's keys or submit unless it is disabled, an open popover's or dialog's keys or dismiss, else the mod's own keys) and select (the option of that name inside the element: an item, button or clickable row, by its whole name, else the only one whose name has it). One that does nothing says why. A step the window does not take within 5 s fails, and is never carried out later.

The app's own providers reach any mod; a miniapp's provider reaches only the mods of its own namespace (<namespace>:...), whatever its view mounts: another mod drawn inside it is left out of the tree.

Each component has a 64 MiB aggregate linear-memory cap and a fresh fuel budget per call (currently 2 billion Wasmtime fuel units, not a wall-clock deadline). Bound histories, collections and computation accordingly. There are no preopened directories or inherited environment variables; adding a crate does not grant access to the machine.

The running component is sandboxed; the build is not. Cargo runs as the user. Moonframe refuses provider/local-dependency build scripts, build-dependencies, .cargo folders and toolchains named by path, and builds outside the provider's directory. Proc macros and published dependencies' build scripts can still execute during compilation. Review source and dependencies before building a provider from elsewhere.

Package and share

For source development, keep provider.toml, Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, src/ and the local wit/ together. Other developers need Rust and the wasm32-wasip2 target.

For a prebuilt distribution, the runtime needs only:

providers/counter/
  provider.toml
  provider.wasm

Copy the built counter.wasm to the literal filename provider.wasm in a separate staging folder beside its manifest. Leave Cargo.toml out of that staged folder so machines with Cargo do not rebuild it. Keep your development sources. The component is portable across the platforms supported by the matching Moonframe host interface.

In the cloned starter, just stage stages the built-in app/ with its WASM providers prebuilt; just bundle uses that staging step. For an app on the library, cargo run --release -- bundle also packages its WASM providers. See building and bundling apps for profile bundles.

Git packages installed with moonframe app install or moonframe mod install are source-only: they reject binary files, including provider.wasm. Ship source through those commands; prebuilt components belong in bundled releases or manually staged app folders. Do not include target/ or compiled components in a source package.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Check
Nothing builds; app.counter stays nil Is the mod drawn, and does its view read app.counter? Does the shell place its region? Check the red problem pill at the top of the window and the terminal log.
Cannot find std for the target Install wasm32-wasip2 for the toolchain actually building the provider.
Cannot find the WIT file The macro path is relative to the provider crate root. Keep wit/provider.wit inside it.
Missing exports or component instantiation error Use wasm32-wasip2, the matching WIT, all three Guest methods and export!(Counter).
Source build fails despite a provider.wasm Source takes precedence when Cargo is available; fix the build or use a separate prebuilt-only staging folder.
start: initial must be… Fix [settings] initial; a start error prevents the first tick.
Invalid JSON, memory error or fuel exhaustion Return valid, bounded JSON and limit work per call; inspect the provider's error.
system_load returns an error Put capabilities = ["system"] before [settings].
No data in a custom library app Ensure its wasm Cargo feature is enabled; without it providers publish nothing and report the disabled feature on a message.

Coding-agent recipe

When asked to build a WASM provider:

  1. Identify the app folder and choose an unused provider name. Confirm that WASM's available capabilities cover the task.
  2. Copy the matching WIT locally; create an independent cdylib crate with kind = "wasm". Keep manifest keys separate from [settings].
  3. Define the published JSON shape and accepted message payloads before writing the view, in types.luau (Published, Message) with an example published.json and a test holding tick to it. Validate settings and handle unknown messages.
  4. Implement start, tick, receive and export!. Publish whole snapshots, bound work and memory, and do not assume runtime state persists.
  5. Read app.<name> with a nil fallback; send payloads with send "provider:<name>" { ... }. Follow the Moonframe and component skills for UI.
  6. Build for wasm32-wasip2, run the app's headless checks and Luau type checks where configured, then verify startup, a message and reload. State explicitly when an interactive check was not performed.
  7. Keep source packages and prebuilt release staging distinct. Link to this guide instead of duplicating a different provider protocol.

Further examples: system uses the host capability; Gantry telemetry keeps a larger in-memory model and handles messages (its data is simulated).
